title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
summary: Learn what cloud computing is, the IaaS, PaaS and SaaS models, core services and cost estimates, shared-responsibility security, scaling and availability, and how to manage cloud costs and careers.
audience: Students, IT support staff, developers and business people moving systems online

body.p: Cloud computing means renting computing resources (servers, storage, databases, networking and software) over the internet, paying for what you use, instead of buying and running your own machines. A student storing files online, a bank running its app and a start-up training an AI model can all use the same large data centres run by cloud providers.

list: On-demand self-service: create resources yourself in minutes through a website or code.
Broad network access: use them from anywhere over the internet.
Resource pooling: providers share huge pools of hardware among many customers.
Rapid elasticity: scale up for busy periods and down again afterwards.
Measured service: usage is metered and billed, like electricity.
No large upfront hardware purchase; costs become operating expenses.
Fast experimentation and global reach.
Managed services reduce the work of patching and maintaining systems.
Built-in options for backup, disaster recovery and security.

body.tip: The cloud is still somebody else's computer: you gain convenience but must manage costs, security settings and data location carefully.

body.p: Cloud services are offered at different levels of control and responsibility.

list: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent virtual machines, storage and networks and manage the operating system and software yourself.
PaaS (Platform as a Service): the provider runs the servers and operating system; you deploy your code or database. Examples include managed databases and app-hosting platforms.
SaaS (Software as a Service): complete applications used through a browser, such as email, office suites and accounting software.
Serverless (Functions as a Service): you upload small functions that run only when triggered and are billed per execution.
Public cloud: shared infrastructure from a provider, open to any customer.
Private cloud: cloud-style infrastructure used by one organisation, on its premises or hosted.
Hybrid cloud: a mix, for example keeping sensitive records on-premises while running a website in the public cloud.
Multi-cloud: using more than one provider.

body.p: Moving from IaaS to SaaS, you manage less and the provider manages more, but you also have less control over how things work.

body.tip: Ask "who patches the operating system?" If you do, it is IaaS; if the provider does and you supply code, it is PaaS.

body.p: Most cloud solutions are built from a few building blocks. Compute runs your code: virtual machines, containers or serverless functions. Storage keeps data: object storage for files and backups, block storage as virtual disks, and file storage shared between machines. Networking connects things securely: virtual networks, firewalls, load balancers and content delivery networks (CDNs). Databases store structured data: relational (SQL) and NoSQL services, often fully managed.

Prices vary by provider and region, so always use the provider's calculator, but the arithmetic is simple. Storing 500 GB at an example price of $0.023 per GB per month costs 500 x 0.023 = $11.50 a month. Two virtual machines at $0.05 an hour, running all month (about 730 hours), cost 2 x 0.05 x 730 = $73. Committing to one year in advance with a 40% discount would cut that to $43.80.

list: Data transferred out to the internet is often charged; data coming in is usually free.
Turn off development machines at night and weekends.
Pick the right size: an idle large machine wastes money every hour.

body.tip: Use object storage for files and images rather than storing them on a virtual machine's disk; it is cheaper and far more durable.

lessons.title: Cloud security and the shared responsibility model

body.p: Security in the cloud is shared. The provider secures the physical data centres, hardware and core infrastructure. The customer is responsible for how they configure and use services: user accounts, permissions, data, network rules and their own applications. Most cloud breaches come from customer misconfiguration, such as a storage bucket accidentally left public.

list: Identity and access management: give each person their own account and only the permissions they need (least privilege).
Turn on multi-factor authentication, especially for administrator accounts.
Never put passwords or secret keys in code or public repositories; use the provider's secrets manager.
Encrypt data at rest and in transit (HTTPS).
Log and monitor activity, and set alerts for unusual behaviour.
Back up important data and test restoring it.

body.p: Personal data stored in the cloud is still covered by laws such as POPIA in South Africa, the Nigeria Data Protection Act and Kenya's Data Protection Act. Some laws or contracts require certain data to stay in particular countries, so choose regions deliberately. Several major providers now run data centres in Africa, for example in South Africa.

body.tip: Review permissions regularly and remove accounts of people who have left; old unused keys are a favourite route for attackers.

body.p: Cloud systems are designed to handle changing demand and to survive failures. Vertical scaling makes a machine bigger; horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer, which spreads requests between them. Auto-scaling adds or removes machines automatically based on load, such as CPU use.

Availability is the share of time a service works. 99.9% ("three nines") allows about (1 - 0.999) x 8760 = 8.76 hours of downtime a year; 99.99% allows about 52.6 minutes. Components in a chain multiply: two parts each 99.9% available give about 0.999 x 0.999 = 99.8%. Duplicates in parallel help: if each of two independent servers is down 1% of the time, both are down together only 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.01% of the time, so at least one is up 99.99% of the time.

list: Regions are separate geographic areas; availability zones are isolated data centres within a region.
Spread critical systems across zones so one failure does not take everything down.
Use health checks so load balancers stop sending traffic to failed machines.
Plan disaster recovery: how much data you can lose (RPO) and how fast you must recover (RTO).

body.tip: Choose a region close to your users to reduce latency; serving Nigerian users from a European region adds noticeable delay.

lessons.title: Managing costs, migration and cloud careers

body.p: Cloud bills can surprise people because everything is metered. Good cost management (often called FinOps) makes spending visible and controlled.

list: Set budgets and billing alerts from day one.
Tag resources by project and owner so you can see who spends what.
Right-size machines and delete unused disks, snapshots and test environments.
Use reserved or committed-use discounts for steady workloads and spot or pre-emptible machines for interruptible jobs.
Watch data-transfer charges between regions and to the internet.

body.p: Common migration approaches are rehosting (lift and shift), replatforming (small changes, such as moving to a managed database) and refactoring (redesigning applications to use cloud-native services). Start with a pilot, measure performance and cost, and train staff.

Cloud skills are in high demand: cloud support, administration, DevOps, security and solutions architecture. Providers offer free tiers for practice and entry-level certifications. Combine them with Linux, networking, scripting and Git skills.

body.tip: Practise on a free tier, but set a billing alert first so a forgotten resource cannot run up a bill.
